name: Halo effect
statement: One favourable impression of a person spreads to judgements it has nothing to do with, so someone who looks the part is rated as more capable too.
meaning: The claim is about contamination between ratings that ought to be independent. If a rater scores a person on a list of separate qualities and every score moves with every other, either the qualities really do travel together in people, or the rater formed one overall impression and read it off once per line. Thorndike's argument was that the correlations were too high and too even to be the first. What makes the effect awkward to study is that this is a claim about the difference between real covariation and rated covariation, and measuring the real thing is exactly what the ratings were supposed to do.

origin.note: The paper is "A constant error in psychological ratings". Officers rated their subordinates on physical qualities, intelligence, leadership and personal qualities using a scale devised by Walter Dill Scott, with a fifth section for general value to the service, and instructions that required each qualification to be considered on its own. One flight commander rating 137 aviation cadets correlated intelligence with physique at .51, with leadership at .58 and with character at .64. Across the three raters Thorndike studied next, the average correlations were .31 for physique with intelligence, .39 for physique with leadership and .28 for physique with character. Those three figures are averages over raters, not single coefficients. Thorndike traces the observation back to a 1915 study of employees at two industrial corporations.

evidence: The original evidence is correlational and comes from rating data. Thorndike's sharpest case sits outside the four-way scale. He correlated the total Scott rating of aviation officers with a separate rating of technical ability as a flyer, a quality he argued was specialised, and the eight raters he studied gave .74, .85, .52, .91, .63, .72, .47 and .53, an average of .67. He carried the argument into teaching through Knight's study of 129 teachers rated by their superior officer on the Boyce score card, where general merit correlated .68 with intellect, .79 with power in discipline and .63 with voice, and voice itself correlated .63 with intelligence. Nisbett and Wilson supplied the experimental version. They showed 118 University of Michigan students, 62 men and 56 women, one of two videotaped interviews of about seven minutes with the same instructor, a native French-speaking Belgian who spoke English with a fairly pronounced accent. In one interview he was warm and flexible, in the other cold and doctrinaire. Liking moved as intended, 5.48 against 3.18 on an eight-point scale, t = 8.62, p < .00001. Ratings of features he had not altered moved with it: physical appearance t = 4.71 and p < .00001, mannerisms t = 4.06 and p < .0001, accent t = 3.78 and p < .0002, each on df of 1/117. The paper states that all its p values are two-tailed. A follow-up showed 34 further students the tapes without the sound, and appearance and mannerisms came out only trivially higher in the warm version, t below 1 for both, which is the paper's ground for treating the attributes as constant. Subjects denied the influence. Of 34 asked whether their liking had shifted their attribute ratings, a majority said it had not, and the paper reports all six one-sample t tests as not significant. Of 56 asked the reverse question, those who had seen the cold instructor said their view of his appearance, mannerisms and accent had lowered their liking, t = 3.28, 2.80 and 2.74, all p < .01. The physical attractiveness branch is a separate and larger literature with meta-analyses of its own, and it is set out at the physical attractiveness stereotype, no. 505, rather than repeated here.

replication.headline: The experimental effect has been repeated, once against subjects who were told what it was, and the index built from it for workplace ratings is what has been attacked.
replication.detail: Wetzel, Wilson and Kort repeated the Nisbett and Wilson design and pushed against it. Subjects again watched a warm or a cold interview with a college instructor and then rated his physical appearance, mannerisms and French accent. Some were told to introspect on their own thinking as they watched, and others were told what the halo effect was and given a reason either to show it or not to show it. Their abstract reports that subjects in every condition were susceptible. Warm-version viewers rated the three attributes higher than cold-version viewers even when informed and forewarned, the instructions changed nothing about awareness, and subjects in all conditions said their liking had had only a minimal effect on their ratings. Only that abstract was obtained, so no figure from the paper appears here. Gräf and Unkelbach ran four experiments on agency and communion traits and found halo transfer from positive information both within and across those two dimensions, and transfer from negative information only within them. Their full text was closed as well. What is contested is the measure rather than the observation. Murphy, Jako and Anhalt set out the definition of halo error that dominated the twentieth century in four parts: that it was common, that it was a rater error with true and illusory components, that it inflated correlations among rating dimensions through a general evaluation, and that its consequences were bad. Their abstract says all of the major elements of that conception are either wrong or problematic, and asks for a moratorium on using halo indices as dependent measures in applied research. The difficulty is the one built into Thorndike's argument. Calling a correlation between rated traits an error requires knowing what the true correlation is, and in an appraisal system nobody does.

study.cite: Wetzel, C. G., Wilson, T. D., & Kort, J. (1981). The halo effect revisited: Forewarned is not forearmed. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 17(4), 427-439.

limits: No standardised effect sizes are printed here. Thorndike reports correlations, Nisbett and Wilson report t values and a figure whose bars carry the percentages, and the numbers in the two closed replications were not obtained. Three articles stayed behind paywalls on 17 August 2026. Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar and open-web searches returned the records and the abstracts for Wetzel, Wilson and Kort, for Gräf and Unkelbach, and for Eagly and colleagues, and no copy of any of the three. The same search returned no full text for Murphy, Jako and Anhalt, whose abstract was read at the publisher. Everything attributed to those four papers here is their abstract's own wording. Westbury and King offer a reading of the correlation that does not require a rater error at all. Thirty-nine participants, 36 of them analysed, judged how likely a person was to be rated highly on both traits in each of 126 trait-word pairs, and the cosine similarity of the two words in a word2vec model predicted those judgements at a cross-validated r squared of .19. Adding the frequency of the more common word and the valence of the less positive word took it to .447 cross-validated, which they put at 93% of the systematic variance available. Those are judgements about pairs of trait words, not ratings of a person anybody met, and that is the limit of what they show. Two literatures also run together under the one name: impression contamination in experiments, and halo error in workplace ratings. They have different evidence and different problems.
misreadings: The halo effect is often stated as though attractiveness causes people to be judged better at everything. Eagly and colleagues put the qualification in the title of their meta-analysis, and the physical attractiveness stereotype, no. 505, carries what it found. Thorndike's own paper is the second casualty of retelling. He ran no experiment. He analysed rating sheets that officers and school superiors had filled in for real decisions about salaries and promotions, and his word halo describes ratings of particular qualities being suffused by a general impression of the person. The term is also used interchangeably with the horn effect, no. 175, its negative counterpart, though the two have not been shown to be symmetrical and that entry carries the evidence. In business writing it has drifted into meaning any spillover of reputation between products, which is a claim about brands rather than a finding about how raters rate people.

sources.text: Thorndike, E. L. (1920). A constant error in psychological ratings. Journal of Applied Psychology, 4(1), 25-29. Read in full from a scan hosted by MIT, downloaded twice to the same checksum.

Nisbett, R. E., & Wilson, T. D. (1977). The halo effect: Evidence for unconscious alteration of judgments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(4), 250-256. Read in full from the scan linked here, and every figure quoted was confirmed against a second independent scan.

Wetzel, C. G., Wilson, T. D., & Kort, J. (1981). The halo effect revisited: Forewarned is not forearmed. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 17(4), 427-439. A replication and extension of Nisbett and Wilson by one of its authors. Closed access; only the publisher abstract was read.

Gräf, M., & Unkelbach, C. (2016). Halo effects in trait assessment depend on information valence: Why being honest makes you industrious, but lying does not make you lazy. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 42(3), 290-310. Closed access; the abstract was read at PubMed.

Murphy, K. R., Jako, R. A., & Anhalt, R. L. (1993). Nature and consequences of halo error: A critical analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 78(2), 218-225. Closed access; the four-part definition and the moratorium are read from the publisher's abstract at the link given.

Eagly, A. H., Ashmore, R. D., Makhijani, M. G., & Longo, L. C. (1991). What is beautiful is good, but...: A meta-analytic review of research on the physical attractiveness stereotype. Psychological Bulletin, 110(1), 109-128. Closed access on every attempt. Nothing on this page rests on it beyond its title.
Westbury, C., & King, D. (2024). A constant error, revisited: A new explanation of the halo effect. Cognitive Science, 48(12), e70022. Open access. Read from the JATS XML at PubMed Central.
